Chapter 8: The Decline of Convict Leasing and Peonage—Economic Shifts and Changing Attitudes
By the 1920s, everything was shifting. The South, which had long felt cut off and deeply tied to agriculture, started connecting with the rest of the country in new ways. Factories were popping up, new technologies arrived, and fresh ideas began to take hold. The old systems of forced labor—though they still had a grip—were facing challenges from places no one really expected.
In bustling cities, factories and mills opened doors to new kinds of work. Black families, hoping for something better, joined the Great Migration and moved north—leaving behind the fields and the harsh labor camps of the rural South. As the labor market changed, so did the logic behind convict leasing and peonage. Why stick with forced labor when there were more and more free workers ready to take jobs?
At the same time, public attitudes were starting to shift. The ugly reality of convict leasing and debt peonage—once hidden away—was getting harder to ignore. Reporters published shocking stories, reformers pushed for change, and a new wave of activists began to demand an end to these old, brutal systems. The moral cost of forced labor, which some had tried to excuse or just deny, was now making people uneasy. For some, it was a source of deep shame. For others, it became a reason to fight for something better.
Picture this: in a small town, a group of local women decided enough was enough. They started a campaign to shut down a notorious prison camp. They wrote letters, organized meetings, and challenged officials at every turn. Even though they ran into plenty of resistance, their efforts finally paid off—the camp closed its doors for good. It might have been a small victory, but it was a sign that things were starting to change.
State governments felt the pressure. Reformers were getting louder, and the economy was moving in a new direction. One by one, states began phasing out convict leasing. Sure, some replaced it with chain gangs—which wasn’t much of an improvement—but it was clear the old system was crumbling. The federal government got involved too, passing new laws to end peonage and protect workers’ rights. Was enforcement perfect? Not even close. But the momentum was building, and it was impossible to ignore.
When you look back, it’s clear that the end of forced labor didn’t come from one dramatic moment. It was all these small changes—economic, social, and political—adding up, making the old ways impossible to keep going. The struggle was far from finished, but finally, the worst abuses were being forced out into the light, and slowly, brought to an end.
